package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via email, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: FTCode is a malicious PowerShell-based ransomware distributed via spam campaigns. It is delivered through malicious Word documents containing macros that execute PowerShell commands to download and run ransomware, encrypting user files and demanding payment for decryption. The attack chain leverages Office macros to bypass security controls and execute remote code, resulting in data loss and extortion.

execution_context.trigger: At document open, when the user enables macros
execution_context.file_location: Embedded macro in Word document (e.g., invoice.docm, inside VBA project)
required_permissions: network (if PowerShell is used to download payloads)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Sub AutoOpen()
  Dim objShell As Object
  Set objShell = CreateObject("Wscript.Shell")
  objShell.Run "powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command [malicious PowerShell command]"
End Sub
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document open, the macro executes, launching a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, which initiates the download and execution of a remote ransomware payload, resulting in the infection of the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The macro uses AutoOpen to trigger automatically when the document is opened, and launches PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and NoProfile, which are common techniques to evade security controls and execute malicious code without user awareness.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not invoke PowerShell with bypassed security settings or execute hidden processes that download and run code from the internet.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise automation may use macros to launch trusted scripts, but never to download and execute untrusted code from external sources or with security bypasses.
key_indicators: AutoOpen macro triggers on document open
Use of Wscript.Shell to launch PowerShell
ExecutionPolicy Bypass and NoProfile flags in PowerShell command
Hidden window style to conceal execution
Command string includes download and execution of remote code

execution_context.trigger: At PowerShell process start, after macro execution
execution_context.file_location: PowerShell command line (spawned by macro from Word document)
required_permissions: network (to download ransomware payload and potentially communicate with C2)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At PowerShell process start, the command downloads a remote script from a malicious domain using DownloadString, immediately executes it in memory via IEX, resulting in the FTCode ransomware payload running and encrypting user files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The command downloads and executes a remote script in memory, a hallmark of fileless malware delivery. The use of IEX with DownloadString from an external domain is a well-known technique for bypassing disk-based detection and rapidly deploying ransomware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell usage should not fetch and execute code from untrusted remote sources, especially with hidden execution and security bypass flags.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use similar commands for internal automation, but only with trusted internal sources and never with obfuscated or hidden execution from unknown domains.
key_indicators: Immediate execution of downloaded code via IEX
Hidden window style to avoid user detection
URL points to known FTCode infrastructure or suspicious domain

attack_chain.action: User receives a spam email with a malicious Word document attachment.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens the document and enables macros.

attack_chain.action: Malicious macro executes upon document open, launching a hidden PowerShell process with security bypass flags.
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell process is started, which downloads and executes the ransomware payload.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell downloads and executes the FTCode ransomware script from a remote server using DownloadString and IEX.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware encrypts user files and displays a ransom note demanding payment for decryption.

behavioral_signatures: Office documents (e.g., .docm) containing macros that invoke PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and NoProfile
PowerShell processes launched by Office applications with hidden window style
PowerShell commands that use DownloadString and IEX to fetch and execute remote scripts
Unusual process tree: Office application -> PowerShell -> network activity
file_indicators: Office documents with embedded macros (e.g., .docm, .xlsm) received via email
Presence of FTCode-related PowerShell scripts (e.g., ftcode.ps1) on disk or in memory
Ransom note files created by FTCode (e.g., README.txt, with ransom instructions)
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to suspicious or known malicious domains hosting ftcode.ps1
PowerShell user-agent strings in network logs indicating script download
Connections to domains or IPs associated with FTCode campaigns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents containing macros that invoke PowerShell with ExecutionPolicy Bypass and NoProfile flags, especially when launched with hidden window style. Detect PowerShell processes spawned by Office applications that use DownloadString and IEX to fetch and execute scripts from external sources. Flag outbound HTTP requests to known FTCode infrastructure or suspicious domains. Use endpoint protection to block or alert on suspicious macro and PowerShell activity, and scan for FTCode-related ransom notes or scripts on disk.
